title: Measures for Performance Evaluation of ML Algorithms

toc.title: 5.1 Classification accuracy and the confusion matrix
5.6 Box plots and variability of results
5.10 Multi-class problems and the precision-recall trade-off
Model answers: medium (5 marks) and long (10 marks) questions

html:
A cancer-screening model reports "99 percent accuracy". If only 1 percent of patients have cancer, a program that says "healthy" to everybody scores exactly that, and misses every sick patient.

Choosing the right measure is as important as choosing the algorithm.

This unit gives the standard measures for classifiers (accuracy, the confusion matrix, costs, sensitivity and specificity, precision and recall, ROC curves), and the statistics (box plots, confidence intervals, cross-validation) that tell you whether a difference between two models is real.

What this unit gives you
  • Classification accuracy and the confusion matrix, and when accuracy misleads.
  • Misclassification costs and cost-sensitive decisions.
  • Sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall and the F1 score.
  • The ROC curve, the area under it, and how to build it from scores.
  • Box plots, confidence intervals and k-fold cross-validation, ending with a template for the course mini-project.

5.1 Classification accuracy and the confusion matrix

A confusion matrix counts predictions against truth. For a binary problem with a positive class (the one we want to detect: disease, fraud, spam):

Predicted positive Predicted negative
Actual positive True positive (TP) False negative (FN)
Actual negative False positive (FP) True negative (TN)

\text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}, \qquad \text{Error rate}=1-\text{Accuracy}.

For more than two classes the matrix is c\times c: the diagonal holds correct predictions and the off-diagonal cells show which classes are confused with which.

When accuracy misleads. With class imbalance accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class. A fraud detector on 10,000 transactions with 20 frauds that flags nothing has accuracy 99.8 percent and detects no fraud.

Use the measures below, and always compare with a baseline such as "always predict the majority class".

5.2 Misclassification costs

The two errors rarely cost the same. A false negative in cancer screening (a missed cancer) is far worse than a false positive (an extra test).

A cost matrix assigns a cost to every cell (correct predictions usually cost 0) and the total cost is C=c_{FP}\cdot FP+c_{FN}\cdot FN. The best model for the business is the one with the lowest cost, which may not be the most accurate.

Two ways to build it in: train as usual and move the decision threshold (flag as positive when the probability exceeds c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN}), from the minimum-risk rule of Unit 3), or give the costly class a higher weight during training.

5.3 Sensitivity, specificity, recall and precision

Measure Formula Question it answers
Sensitivity = recall = true-positive rate (TPR) \dfrac{TP}{TP+FN} Of all actual positives, how many did we catch?
Specificity = true-negative rate (TNR) \dfrac{TN}{TN+FP} Of all actual negatives, how many did we correctly clear?
Precision (positive predictive value) \dfrac{TP}{TP+FP} Of all that we flagged, how many were truly positive?
False-positive rate (FPR) \dfrac{FP}{FP+TN}=1-\text{specificity} Of all actual negatives, how many did we wrongly flag?
F1 score \dfrac{2PR}{P+R} Harmonic mean of precision P and recall R

Recall and precision pull in opposite directions: flagging more cases raises recall and lowers precision. The harmonic mean punishes a big gap: precision 1.0 with recall 0.1 gives F1 = 0.18, not 0.55.

Use recall when misses are costly (disease, fraud) and precision when false alarms are costly (spam filter blocking real mail).

A screening test on 100 people (50 ill, 50 healthy)

TP = 40, FN = 10, FP = 5, TN = 45. Accuracy = 85/100 = 0.85. Sensitivity = 40/50 = 0.80. Specificity = 45/50 = 0.90. Precision = 40/45 = 0.889. F1 = 2(0.889)\dfrac{0.80}{0.889+0.80} = 0.842.

If a missed case costs Rs 50 and a false alarm Rs 5: total cost = 10(50) + 5(5) = Rs 525, average Rs 5.25 per person.

def report(TP, FN, FP, TN, c_fn=50, c_fp=5):
    n = TP + FN + FP + TN
    P = TP / (TP + FP) if TP + FP else 0.0; R = TP / (TP + FN)
    print("accuracy %.3f | sensitivity %.3f | specificity %.3f | precision %.3f | F1 %.3f | cost %d"
          % ((TP + TN) / n, R, TN / (TN + FP), P, 2 * P * R / (P + R) if P + R else 0, c_fn * FN + c_fp * FP))
report(40, 10, 5, 45)
print("imbalanced: 10 ill in 1000, classifier always says healthy")
report(0, 10, 0, 990)

accuracy 0.850 | sensitivity 0.800 | specificity 0.900 | precision 0.889 | F1 0.842 | cost 525
imbalanced: 10 ill in 1000, classifier always says healthy
accuracy 0.990 | sensitivity 0.000 | specificity 1.000 | precision 0.000 | F1 0.000 | cost 500

5.4 The ROC curve

Most classifiers output a score (probability) and a threshold turns it into a class. Moving the threshold trades sensitivity against specificity.

The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) plots TPR (y) against FPR (x) for every threshold. The corner (0,1) is perfect; the diagonal is random guessing; a curve bowed towards the top-left is better.

The area under the curve (AUC) summarises the curve in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random, and AUC equals the probability that a random positive receives a higher score than a random negative.

Construction. Sort examples by score from high to low, then start at (0,0) and move up one step for every positive and right one step for every negative.

Ten scored examples

Positives have scores 0.95, 0.85, 0.70, 0.60, 0.45 and negatives 0.80, 0.55, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20. Sorted: 0.95(P), 0.85(P), 0.80(N), 0.70(P), 0.60(P), 0.55(N), 0.45(P), 0.40(N), 0.30(N), 0.20(N).

Each positive step is 1/5=0.2 up and each negative step 1/5=0.2 right. Counting, for each positive, the negatives below it: 5, 5, 4, 4, 3, total 21 of 25 pairs, so AUC =21/25=0.84.

pos = [0.95, 0.85, 0.70, 0.60, 0.45]; neg = [0.80, 0.55, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20]
pts = [(0.0, 0.0)]; tp = fp = 0
for score, lab in sorted([(s, 1) for s in pos] + [(s, 0) for s in neg], reverse=True):
    tp += lab; fp += 1 - lab
    pts.append((fp / len(neg), tp / len(pos)))
print("ROC points (FPR, TPR):", pts)
auc = sum((x2 - x1) * (y1 + y2) / 2 for (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in zip(pts, pts[1:]))
pairs = sum(p > n for p in pos for n in neg)
print("AUC by trapezoids = %.2f, by pair counting = %d/25 = %.2f" % (auc, pairs, pairs / 25))
for th in (0.9, 0.65, 0.5, 0.35):
    tpr = sum(p >= th for p in pos) / 5; fpr = sum(n >= th for n in neg) / 5
    print("threshold %.2f -> TPR %.1f, FPR %.1f" % (th, tpr, fpr))

ROC points (FPR, TPR): [(0.0, 0.0), (0.0, 0.2), (0.0, 0.4), (0.2, 0.4), (0.2, 0.6), (0.2, 0.8), (0.4, 0.8), (0.4, 1.0), (0.6, 1.0), (0.8, 1.0), (1.0, 1.0)]
AUC by trapezoids = 0.84, by pair counting = 21/25 = 0.84
threshold 0.90 -> TPR 0.2, FPR 0.0
threshold 0.65 -> TPR 0.6, FPR 0.2
threshold 0.50 -> TPR 0.8, FPR 0.4
threshold 0.35 -> TPR 1.0, FPR 0.6

5.5 Regression measures

For numeric predictions, with errors e_i=\hat y_i-y_i, the common measures are MAE =\frac1N\sum|e_i| (average size of error, in the units of y), MSE =\frac1N\sum e_i^2 and RMSE =\sqrt{\text{MSE}} (both punish big errors), and the coefficient of determination

R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum e_i^{2}}{\sum (y_i-\bar y)^{2}},

the share of variance explained (0 means no better than predicting the mean). RMSE is at least MAE; a large gap means a few big errors.

5.6 Box plots and variability of results

One accuracy number hides how much a model varies.

Run the evaluation several times (different folds or random splits) and show the spread with a box plot, which draws the five-number summary: minimum, first quartile Q_1, median, third quartile Q_3 and maximum.

The box covers Q_1 to Q_3 (the middle 50 percent), a line marks the median, and the whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5\times\text{IQR} of the box, where \text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1.

Points beyond the whiskers are plotted individually as outliers.

import numpy as np
A = np.array([0.82, 0.85, 0.84, 0.86, 0.83, 0.85, 0.87, 0.84, 0.83, 0.85])
B = np.array([0.80, 0.90, 0.78, 0.88, 0.82, 0.92, 0.75, 0.86, 0.89, 0.79])
for name, v in (("Model A", A), ("Model B", B)):
    q1, med, q3 = np.percentile(v, [25, 50, 75])
    print(name, "min %.3f Q1 %.4f median %.3f Q3 %.4f max %.3f | IQR %.4f | mean %.3f sd %.3f" % (v.min(), q1, med, q3, v.max(), q3 - q1, v.mean(), v.std(ddof=1)))

Model A min 0.820 Q1 0.8325 median 0.845 Q3 0.8500 max 0.870 | IQR 0.0175 | mean 0.844 sd 0.015
Model B min 0.750 Q1 0.7925 median 0.840 Q3 0.8875 max 0.920 | IQR 0.0950 | mean 0.839 sd 0.058

5.7 Confidence intervals

A test accuracy of 0.85 on 100 cases is an estimate of the true accuracy. A confidence interval gives a range likely to contain the truth.

Treat each test case as an independent success/failure with true accuracy p; the sample proportion \hat p has standard error \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n} and the 95 percent confidence interval (normal approximation, valid when n\hat p and n(1-\hat p) exceed about 10) is

\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p\,(1-\hat p)}{n}}.

For 90 percent use 1.645 and for 99 percent 2.576. For the mean of k cross-validation scores use \bar x\pm t\,s/\sqrt k with the t value for k-1 degrees of freedom.

Intervals that overlap heavily mean the data cannot show that one model is better; to prove a difference, use a paired test on the same folds.

from math import sqrt
for n in (100, 400, 1000):
    p = 0.85; se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
    print("n = %4d  accuracy 0.85  95%% CI = [%.3f, %.3f]  (+/- %.3f)" % (n, p - 1.96 * se, p + 1.96 * se, 1.96 * se))
n_needed = (1.96 / 0.02) ** 2 * 0.85 * 0.15
print("test cases needed for +/- 0.02:", round(n_needed))

n =  100  accuracy 0.85  95% CI = [0.780, 0.920]  (+/- 0.070)
n =  400  accuracy 0.85  95% CI = [0.815, 0.885]  (+/- 0.035)
n = 1000  accuracy 0.85  95% CI = [0.828, 0.872]  (+/- 0.022)
test cases needed for +/- 0.02: 1225

5.8 Cross-validation and fair evaluation

k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k equal folds (usually k=5 or 10). Each fold serves once as the validation set while the model is trained on the other k-1; the k scores are averaged.

All data is used for both training and validation, and the spread of the scores shows the variability. Stratified folds keep the class proportions in every fold, essential with imbalance; leave-one-out (k=N) is nearly unbiased but slow.

Rules for fair evaluation: split before any scaling, feature selection or balancing (otherwise validation information leaks into training); never tune on the test set; report the baseline; report more than accuracy; and give the interval, not just a single number.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
X = np.r_[rng.normal(0, 1, (60, 2)), rng.normal(2, 1, (60, 2))]; y = np.r_[np.zeros(60), np.ones(60)]
idx = rng.permutation(120); folds = np.array_split(idx, 5); scores = []
for i in range(5):
    te = folds[i]; tr = np.concatenate([folds[j] for j in range(5) if j != i])
    c0 = X[tr][y[tr] == 0].mean(axis=0); c1 = X[tr][y[tr] == 1].mean(axis=0)
    pred = (np.linalg.norm(X[te] - c1, axis=1) < np.linalg.norm(X[te] - c0, axis=1)).astype(float)
    scores.append((pred == y[te]).mean())
print("fold accuracies:", np.round(scores, 3), "mean %.3f sd %.3f" % (np.mean(scores), np.std(scores, ddof=1)))

fold accuracies: [1.    1.    0.875 0.917 0.875] mean 0.933 sd 0.063

5.9 Laboratory work and the mini-project

The syllabus requires laboratory work on every unit and a small project in Python or MATLAB. A sound template:

Step What to do Unit
1. Problem and data State the task (for example, predict student pass/fail), collect or choose a data set, describe each feature 1
2. Clean and explore Handle missing values, plot distributions, check class balance 1, 5
3. Split Train, validation and test (or cross-validation) 1
4. Baselines and models Majority-class baseline, then two or three of: regression, tree, k-NN, naive Bayes, SVM, small neural network 2, 3
5. Structure Optionally cluster or reduce with PCA and plot 4
6. Evaluate Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, ROC and AUC, cross-validated mean with interval 5
7. Report Which model, why, what it cannot do, ethical concerns (bias, privacy) all

Suggested laboratory sequence: (1) statistics and plots with NumPy and matplotlib; (2) linear regression by the normal equation and gradient descent; (3) perceptron on AND, OR, XOR; (4) back-propagation on XOR; (5) ID3 on PlayTennis; (6) naive Bayes on text; (7) k-NN with different k; (8) k-means and hierarchical clustering; (9) PCA on a data set; (10) confusion matrix, ROC and cross-validation of all earlier models.

5.10 Multi-class problems and the precision-recall trade-off

With more than two classes, compute precision, recall and F1 per class (treating that class as positive and the rest as negative) and then combine them.

Macro-average is the plain mean over classes, so every class counts equally; micro-average pools all TP, FP and FN first, so big classes dominate (for single-label problems micro precision, recall and F1 all equal accuracy).

Use macro when the rare classes matter.

import numpy as np
M = np.array([[50, 3, 2], [4, 30, 6], [1, 5, 19]])     # rows: actual class A, B, C; columns: predicted
tp = np.diag(M); fp = M.sum(0) - tp; fn = M.sum(1) - tp
P = tp / (tp + fp); R = tp / (tp + fn); F = 2 * P * R / (P + R)
for c, n in enumerate("ABC"): print("class %s precision %.3f recall %.3f F1 %.3f" % (n, P[c], R[c], F[c]))
print("accuracy %.3f | macro-F1 %.3f | micro-F1 %.3f" % (tp.sum() / M.sum(), F.mean(), 2 * tp.sum() / (2 * tp.sum() + fp.sum() + fn.sum())))

class A precision 0.909 recall 0.909 F1 0.909
class B precision 0.789 recall 0.750 F1 0.769
class C precision 0.704 recall 0.760 F1 0.731
accuracy 0.825 | macro-F1 0.803 | micro-F1 0.825

The trade-off in numbers. Using the ten scores of Section 5.4 as a spam filter, lowering the threshold catches more spam (recall up) but blocks more good mail (precision down).

Choose the threshold by the cost of each error, or by the point on the precision-recall curve that meets a stated target, for example "recall at least 0.8".

pos = [0.95, 0.85, 0.70, 0.60, 0.45]; neg = [0.80, 0.55, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20]
print("threshold  TP FP  precision  recall   F1")
for th in (0.9, 0.75, 0.65, 0.5, 0.35):
    tp = sum(p >= th for p in pos); fp = sum(n >= th for n in neg)
    P = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0; R = tp / 5
    print("%7.2f   %2d %2d  %8.3f  %6.2f  %5.3f" % (th, tp, fp, P, R, 2 * P * R / (P + R) if P + R else 0))

threshold  TP FP  precision  recall   F1
   0.90    1  0     1.000    0.20  0.333
   0.75    2  1     0.667    0.40  0.500
   0.65    3  1     0.750    0.60  0.667
   0.50    4  2     0.667    0.80  0.727

5.11 Summary and exercises

Accuracy hides class imbalance, so read the confusion matrix and use sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall and F1 as the problem demands; weight errors by their costs; the ROC curve and AUC show performance across all thresholds; box plots and confidence intervals show the variability of results; cross-validation with careful splitting gives a fair estimate.

  1. A classifier gives TP = 30, FN = 20, FP = 10, TN = 140. Compute accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1.
  2. Why is accuracy a poor measure for fraud detection? Give a numerical example.
  3. For the matrix in Question 1, with a missed case costing Rs 200 and a false alarm Rs 10, find the total cost.
  4. Explain precision and recall and the trade-off between them. When is each more important?
  5. Construct the ROC curve and AUC for positives 0.9, 0.7, 0.5 and negatives 0.8, 0.4, 0.3.
  6. Compute the 95 percent confidence interval for an accuracy of 0.90 on 200 test cases.
  7. Explain k-fold cross-validation and why stratification matters.
  8. What does a box plot show? Interpret two box plots with equal medians but different box heights.
  9. List the steps of a machine-learning mini-project.

Model answers: medium (5 marks) and long (10 marks) questions

Q1 (5 marks). Measures for TP = 30, FN = 20, FP = 10, TN = 140 (n = 200).

Accuracy =170/200=0.85. Sensitivity =30/50=0.60. Specificity =140/150=0.933. Precision =30/40=0.75. F1 =2(0.75)(0.60)/(1.35)=0.667. Cost with Rs 200 per miss and Rs 10 per false alarm: 20(200)+10(10)= Rs 4,100.

Comment. Accuracy looks good (0.85) but the model misses 40 percent of the positives; with costly misses, a lower threshold is justified.

Q2 (5 marks). ROC and AUC for positives 0.9, 0.7, 0.5 and negatives 0.8, 0.4, 0.3.

Sorted: 0.9(P), 0.8(N), 0.7(P), 0.5(P), 0.4(N), 0.3(N). Each P step is 1/3 up, each N step 1/3 right. Path: (0,0) → (0,1/3) → (1/3,1/3) → (1/3,2/3) → (1/3,1) → (2/3,1) → (1,1).

Pairs with the positive higher: 0.9 beats all 3 negatives; 0.7 beats 0.4 and 0.3 (2); 0.5 beats 0.4 and 0.3 (2); total 7 of 9, so AUC = 7/9 = 0.78.

Q3 (5 marks). 95 percent confidence interval for accuracy 0.90 with n = 200.

SE=\sqrt{0.9(0.1)/200}=\sqrt{0.00045}=0.0212. Margin =1.96\times0.0212=0.0416. Interval =[0.858,\,0.942]. With only 50 cases the margin would be 0.083, which shows why small test sets give unreliable results.

Q4 (10 marks). Explain the confusion matrix and the measures derived from it.

Introduction. The confusion matrix tabulates actual against predicted classes and is the source of all classification measures.

Body. (1) Cells TP, FN, FP, TN. (2) Accuracy (TP+TN)/n, which fails under imbalance. (3) Sensitivity (recall) TP/(TP+FN) and specificity TN/(TN+FP). (4) Precision TP/(TP+FP). (5) F1 =2PR/(P+R). (6) Costs c_{FP}FP+c_{FN}FN.

Example. For TP = 40, FN = 10, FP = 5, TN = 45: accuracy 0.85, recall 0.80, specificity 0.90, precision 0.889, F1 0.842. For 10 ill people in 1,000, a model that predicts "healthy" for everyone has accuracy 0.99 but recall 0.

Conclusion. Report the full matrix and choose the measure that matches the cost of each error.

Q5 (10 marks). Describe k-fold cross-validation and the construction and interpretation of the ROC curve.

Cross-validation. Partition the data into k folds; for each fold train on the other k-1 and test on it; average the k scores and report the mean with its spread or interval.

It uses all data for training and testing and reveals variability; stratification keeps class proportions; all preprocessing must be fitted inside each training fold.

ROC. A model gives scores; a threshold gives a class. Varying the threshold from high to low and plotting TPR against FPR traces the curve from (0,0) to (1,1).

The diagonal is chance, the top-left corner is perfect, and the AUC (0.5 to 1) equals the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. For the ten-example classifier of Section 5.4 the AUC is 0.84.

The curve lets us choose a threshold to suit costs, and compare models independently of any one threshold.

Conclusion. Cross-validation gives a trustworthy estimate of how well the model generalises; the ROC curve shows how it behaves at every operating point.
